explanations.explanation: Dust it is. The LORD says, "Go down and sit in the dust, O Virgin Daughter of Babylon." Then He adds, "Sit on the ground without a throne…" She's going from a throne to the ground, friend. That's a long way down.

A palace sounds right for royalty, I get it. But the LORD sends her the other direction. He says, "Go down and sit in the dust…" and He says she'll sit "…without a throne…" No palace is mentioned anywhere in the verse.

Temple is a fair guess, but the verse never mentions one. The LORD says, "Go down and sit in the dust…" There's no holy building and no fancy chair, just plain ground. I think that's a pretty plain seat for somebody used to a throne.

Nope, friend, that nickname is getting pulled. The LORD says, "For you will no longer be called tender or delicate." It comes right after she's told to sit on the ground without a throne. So the throne goes, and the soft names go with it.

Right, it's False. Babylon is told to "Go down and sit in the dust…" and then the LORD adds, "For you will no longer be called tender or delicate." I'd say a tender, delicate name and a seat in the dust don't go together.
Flour is right. The LORD says, "Take millstones and grind flour…" I know flour well, friend. I've worn it on my apron for years. Grinding it is a long way from sitting on a throne.
Walls are honest work, but that's not this verse. The LORD says, "Take millstones and grind flour…" Millstones are for grinding, not stacking. Nobody's building anything in this one.
No road crew in this verse, friend. The LORD says, "Take millstones and grind flour…" The stones are for grinding. The only thing getting flattened here is her pride.
That's True. The LORD says, "I will take vengeance; I will spare no one." I think this is a heavy line, and it deserves to be heard that way. It comes right after He says her shame will be exposed.
It's True, friend. The LORD says plainly, "I will take vengeance; I will spare no one." I think this is a heavy line. It's right there in verse 3.

Israel is right. The line says, "Our Redeemer—the LORD of Hosts is His name—is the Holy One of Israel." It breaks into the message to Babylon. And it says "Our," so whoever speaks it is counting himself in.

Babylon is who the message is aimed at, so I see the mix-up. But the short line in the middle names a different people. It says the LORD of Hosts is "…the Holy One of Israel." Babylon isn't mentioned in that line at all.

Egypt doesn't show up anywhere in this chapter, friend. The line says, "Our Redeemer—the LORD of Hosts is His name—is the Holy One of Israel." The people named there are Israel. Babylon is the one being spoken to in this chapter.
That's the title. The LORD says, "For you will no longer be called the queen of kingdoms." It's a big, shiny name for an empire. And it's being taken away.

Good try, but that title isn't in this verse. The LORD tells the Daughter of the Chaldeans, "For you will no longer be called the queen of kingdoms." That's the one she loses. Keep your ear on what she's actually called.

That sounds lovely, but it's not what this verse says. The LORD tells her, "For you will no longer be called the queen of kingdoms." That's the title being pulled off her. Nothing in the verse says anything about light.

That's right. The LORD says, "You showed them no mercy…" He adds, "even on the elderly you laid a most heavy yoke." I think this is one of the heavy parts of the passage. It tells us why her fall is coming.
No, friend, it's the opposite. The LORD says, "You showed them no mercy…" Letting them go early would be mercy, and that's not what the verse says. He says even the elderly got "…a most heavy yoke."

Guests get a comfy chair and a warm welcome, and that's not what's described here. The LORD says, "You showed them no mercy…" He also says she laid "…a most heavy yoke." even on the elderly. That's about as far from hospitality as you can get.
It's the opposite, friend. The LORD says, "even on the elderly you laid a most heavy yoke." So going easy on them isn't what the verse says. I think that's a heavy thing to hear.
False is right. The LORD says to Babylon, "even on the elderly you laid a most heavy yoke." She didn't ease up for them. I think that's a heavy detail, and the verse says it plainly.
Queen is right. Babylon says, "I will be queen forever." Forever is a big word to hand yourself. The LORD has already told her she'll lose the title of queen of kingdoms.
Young isn't what she said, friend. Her words were, "I will be queen forever." It's her crown she's sure about, not her age. Nothing in the verse mentions being young.

Humble doesn't match the way she talks. Her words were, "I will be queen forever." I think folks who promise themselves forever aren't usually working on humble. The verse doesn't use that word at all.

It's False, friend. The LORD says, "You did not take these things to heart or consider their outcome." She didn't stop to think where it was heading. That's like sliding a batch in the oven and never checking on it.

False is right. The LORD says, "You did not take these things to heart or consider their outcome." She never stopped to think about where it was all heading. It's like hitting send on a text without rereading it.
That's what she says. The LORD quotes her: "I am, and there is none besides me." She's so sure nobody can touch her. She says it again in verse 10, word for word.

explanations.answer: There is one greater than me
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what she says. The LORD quotes her: "I am, and there is none besides me." Nobody greater is in her picture.

That isn't what the LORD quotes, friend. What she tells herself is, "I am, and there is none besides me." She also says, "I will never be a widow or know the loss of children." Neither line is about her days being numbered.

Widow is right for the first blank. She says, "I will never be a widow or know the loss of children." The LORD answers in verse 9 that widowhood will come upon her. That's a heavy word, so I'll just say it plainly.
Children is right for the second blank. She says she'll never "…know the loss of children." Verse 9 says that loss will come upon her too. I think this is a heavy part of the passage.
Servant isn't in her claim, friend. She says, "I will never be a widow or know the loss of children." Those are the two griefs she names. Being a servant isn't one of them.

Kingdoms comes from a different verse. In verse 5, the LORD says she'll no longer be called "…the queen of kingdoms." But here she says, "I will never be a widow or know the loss of children." Those are the two words that fit.
Wealth isn't what she's bragging about here. She says, "I will never be a widow or know the loss of children." Those are the two griefs she thinks can't touch her. Money doesn't come up in her words.

It's the other way around. The LORD says these losses will come "…in spite of your many sorceries and the potency of your spells." All that effort doesn't hold them back. They come "…in full measure…"
False is right. The LORD says the losses will come "…in full measure, in spite of your many sorceries and the potency of your spells." Her spells don't stop a thing. They come in a single day.
Wisdom is right. The LORD says, "Your wisdom and knowledge led you astray…" What she thought she knew steered her off course. It's like being so sure of your shortcut that you end up lost.
Armies aren't named in this verse. The LORD says, "Your wisdom and knowledge led you astray…" It's her own know-how that misled her. Soldiers aren't part of the sentence.
Gold doesn't come up in this verse, friend. The LORD says, "Your wisdom and knowledge led you astray…" Wisdom and knowledge are the two things named. Nothing shiny in there.
That's it. The LORD says, "you will not know how to charm it away." He adds that she'll be "…unable to ward off." the calamity. Her tricks won't work this time.
Running isn't mentioned here. The LORD says, "you will not know how to charm it away." Charming is the thing she can't do. That fits with her sorceries and spells.
There's no payment plan for this one, friend. The LORD says, "you will not know how to charm it away." Money isn't part of the verse. It's her charms that don't work.

That's how I read it. In verse 11 the LORD says she'll be "…unable to ward off." the calamity. Then in verse 12 He says, "Perhaps you will succeed; perhaps you will inspire terror!" I think that's a dare. He's telling her to go ahead and take her best shot.

That can't be, because of the verse just before. The LORD already said, "A calamity will befall you that you will be unable to ward off." So "Perhaps you will succeed…" isn't a promise. I think it's more like telling her to go ahead and try.

No request to repent shows up in these verses. The LORD says, "So take your stand with your spells and with your many sorceries…" He's telling her to bring out her spells and sorceries. I think it's a dare.
That's True. The LORD says, "let them come forward now and save you…" He's talking about her astrologers, who observe the stars. If they can predict her fate every month, let's see them step up.
It's True, friend. The LORD says to her, "let them come forward now and save you…" He means the astrologers who monthly predict her fate. So He's telling them to step up.
Stubble is right. The LORD says, "Surely they are like stubble; the fire will burn them up." Stubble is the dry leftover that goes up fast. That's a rough comparison for the advisors she trusted.
Gold isn't the picture here. The LORD says, "Surely they are like stubble; the fire will burn them up." Stubble is the thing that burns. It's not something precious.

Stone doesn't fit this verse, friend. The LORD says, "Surely they are like stubble; the fire will burn them up." Stubble goes up in the fire, and it doesn't hold. Stone would stand up better than that.
It's the opposite. The LORD says, "There will be no coals to warm them or fire to sit beside." The astrologers can't deliver themselves from the flame. Nobody's leaving with a cozy campfire.
False is right. The LORD says, "There will be no coals to warm them or fire to sit beside." The fire burns them up, and nothing is left to sit beside. It's no campfire.

That's it. The LORD says, "…each one strays in his own direction; not one of them can save you." These are the folks she labored and traded with since her youth. So they scatter, each going his own way.
That's the opposite of what the LORD says. He says, "…each one strays in his own direction…" Nobody's standing next to her. And then He adds, "not one of them can save you."
Nobody's paying anything here, friend. The LORD says, "…each one strays in his own direction; not one of them can save you." They go their own ways, and none of them rescues her.
